question.prompt: Let \(P(x)=x^{2022}+x^{1011}+1.\) Which of the following polynomials divides \(P(x)?\)

solutions.title: Reduce the large powers
solutions.explanation:
The exponents \(1011\) and \(2022\) leave remainders \(3\) and \(6\) upon division by \(9\). This suggests testing choice E, because
\[
(x^3-1)(x^6+x^3+1)=x^9-1.
\]

Let \(D(x)=x^6+x^3+1\). Write \(F(x)\equiv G(x)\pmod{D(x)}\) to mean that \(F(x)-G(x)\) is a polynomial multiple of \(D(x)\). Adding or multiplying such relations preserves this property, so it lets us simplify powers while keeping track of divisibility.

The displayed identity gives
\[
x^9\equiv1\pmod{D(x)}.
\]
Since \(1011=9\cdot112+3\) and \(2022=9\cdot224+6\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{1011}&=(x^9)^{112}x^3\equiv x^3\pmod{D(x)},\\
x^{2022}&=(x^9)^{224}x^6\equiv x^6\pmod{D(x)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
P(x)\equiv x^6+x^3+1=D(x)\equiv0\pmod{D(x)}.
\]
This means exactly that \(D(x)\) divides \(P(x)\).

The answer is \(\boxed{x^6+x^3+1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutions.title: Interpret the complex roots
solutions.explanation:
The identity
\[
(x^3-1)(x^6+x^3+1)=x^9-1
\]
connects choice E to ninth roots of unity, which are complex numbers whose ninth powers equal \(1\).

The nine numbers
\[
\zeta_k=\cos\frac{2\pi k}{9}+i\sin\frac{2\pi k}{9},
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,8,
\]
are distinct ninth roots of unity. Indeed, multiplication of unit-circle complex numbers adds their angles, so raising each to the ninth power gives angle \(2\pi k\) and value \(1\).

Exactly three of these, those with \(k=0,3,6\), also satisfy \(\zeta_k^3=1\). For each of the remaining six, the displayed factorization gives
\[
\zeta_k^6+\zeta_k^3+1=0,
\]
since \(\zeta_k^3-1\ne0\). These are therefore all six distinct roots of the degree-six polynomial \(D(x)=x^6+x^3+1\).

For any such root \(\zeta\), use \(\zeta^9=1\) to obtain
\[
\zeta^{1011}=\zeta^3,
\qquad
\zeta^{2022}=\zeta^6.
\]
Hence
\[
P(\zeta)=\zeta^6+\zeta^3+1=0.
\]
Every root of \(D\) is thus a root of \(P\). By the factor theorem, the six distinct linear factors belonging to these roots divide \(P\); their product is the monic polynomial \(D\). Therefore \(D\mid P\).

The answer is \(\boxed{x^6+x^3+1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutions.title: Eliminate by integer substitutions
solutions.explanation:
Substituting small integers can turn polynomial divisibility into ordinary integer divisibility, allowing us to rule out choices without handling the large powers directly.

Every candidate has integer coefficients and leading coefficient \(1\), so it is monic. Long division of \(P\) by such a polynomial uses only integer coefficients: each leading term is canceled by subtracting an integer multiple of a power of \(x\) times the divisor. Thus, if a candidate \(F(x)\) divides \(P(x)\), its quotient \(Q(x)\) has integer coefficients. Evaluating \(P(x)=F(x)Q(x)\) at any integer \(t\) shows that \(F(t)\) must divide \(P(t)\), provided \(F(t)\ne0\).

First substitute \(x=-1\). We get
\[
P(-1)=1-1+1=1.
\]
The values of choices A, C, and D at \(-1\) are respectively
\[
3,\qquad 2,\qquad 3.
\]
None divides \(1\), so these three choices are impossible.

To test choice B, substitute \(x=2\). Its value is
\[
2^2+2+1=7.
\]
We only need the remainder of \(P(2)\) upon division by \(7\). Since \(2^3=8\) leaves remainder \(1\), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{2022}&=(2^3)^{674}\equiv1\pmod7,\\
2^{1011}&=(2^3)^{337}\equiv1\pmod7.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
P(2)\equiv1+1+1=3\pmod7,
\]
so \(7\) does not divide \(P(2)\). This eliminates B.

The only remaining choice is \(\boxed{x^6+x^3+1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
